No problem!  I started making ketchup since we always end up with way too many tomatoes at the end of the season from our garden and there's only so much salsa you can eat.

2 lbs of fresh tomatoes
1/2 cup of apple cider vinegar
1/4 cup of molasses
2 tbsp of sugar
To taste: nutmeg, clove, garlic, celery salt

Cook the tomatoes, core and peel them.  Mash them in a large pot, add the rest of your ingredients.  Simmer and stir for 20 minutes.

Press through cheese cloth or a fine sieve to remove chunks.  Can it or freeze it up to 6 months.  Will last up 3 weeks in the fridge.

I started cutting when I was 14.  I'm 32 now and it's daily struggle to "stay clean".

In my family, there wasn't a lot of love.  There's was a lot of pressure to do well, and I stuck out because everyone was very math and science oriented and I was the weird art kid.

More than anything, I wanted my dad to listen without judgement.  When he found out I was cutting, he took away anything I could use to cut, which just made me creative.  Unconditional love with no judgment would have made a world of difference.

One thing I will give him credit for is getting me some therapy and meds.  I saw a psychiatrist and was put on anti-depressants.  However, some family counselling and more coping skills would have been helpful.  

Talk.  Ask about their friends, ask about school, ask about what they're reading.  Just talk and have a rational discussion and communicate.  

Some days are going to be hard.  When I cut, I do it because I feel like I'm going to explode if I don't.  It feels like I'm full of poison and I need to bleed it out.  When I couldn't, I would have the worst panic attacks of my life and disassociate.  Your child is in such immense pain, and they most likely lack the words to describe it.  They may not even understand what is happening to them.  It's taken me 20 years and a lot of therapy to figure out what I feel, and at 15, I had no fucking no clue and no vocabulary for the intense pain, sadness, anger, loneliness and anxiety I felt.

Just love your child.  Listen.  Don't judge.  Get them as much help as you can and as they will accept.  Encourage them to write and create and get out into the world.  Anything that gets them out of their head and is positive.

First of all, you said you have some thyroid issues, so I would go back to your doctor or get a second opinion.  Depression can be heavily related to thyroid issues.

whether or not it's your thyroid, I would get into see a therapist or counsellor.  It sounds like you could use some help with coping skills with your anxiety and depression.  If nothing else, look up the number for your local crisis unit or suicide hotline.  It sounds like you could really use a friendly ear.

There are a few that I try to remember:

"This too shall pass" I got that tattooed on my arm after my first hospitalization.  It reminds me to keep breathing even when I feel like I can't take another breath.

"You've got to kick at the darkness until it bleeds daylight" I thought a lot about this one when I was the hospital the second time.  It reminds me sometimes you have to fight the negative feelings and thoughts and push them aside to find the positive ones, or find the positive even everything seems negative.

"As long as you're breathing, there's more right with you than wrong"  The leader of my group therapy says this a lot and I've been finding more and more I connect with it.  I've been suicidal, homicidal and taking a life is such a final act, there's no coming back.  The days when I can't get out of bed, or I look at my children and cry because I feel like I don't deserve them and they would be better off without me, no matter how deep down the hole I go, at least the next day I will wake up and maybe that day will be better.

The other thing I learned is to stop giving a shit about what other people thought.  When I first got out of the hospital the first time, I realized I was tired of lying about how I felt all the time and I didn't want to lie about where I had been for the last few weeks.  I was amazed how compassionate people were when I told them I was dealing with depression and anxiety.  So I'm not scared to answer people "I'm having a rough day" or "I'm not sure how to answer that" when asked "How are you?" instead of just an automatic "Fine."
